name: Liam Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Liam. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Can you tell me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a blast hole drill at an iron ore mine. It's a big tracked rig that drills rows of holes, about fifteen metres deep, so the shot crew can load them with explosives. I get a drill plan at the start of shift, line up on each marker, drill, move, drill. On a good day I'll do forty-odd holes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what gets you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's mine. Same rig for four years, number 7, I know every rattle. What gets me down is when they change the system on us, like the new tablet for the drill plans last year. Took me three months to stop swearing at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the one we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's the one I'd pick if I got to pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, they oversold it, like they oversell most things. I'm not online much, so it'd be a chat in the crib room. Probably something like, see, number 7 still needs me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. Even without AI, there's talk about drills that run themselves, and some mines have them already. But if it's all slow and boring, I reckon I've got a good fifteen years on this rig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep doing my shifts, keep putting money away for a deposit on a house, maybe back in my home town where it's cheaper. I've got about five months saved, and I'd like ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Just normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some mines already have drills that run themselves. Have you seen one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only on a video a supervisor showed us. A drill moving about with nobody in it, lined up perfect every time. Didn't love that video, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a house back home mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean I've got somewhere that's mine, close to Mum and Dad, with a shed. I'd still fly in and out or drive the four hours. I'm not in a rush, but I like having the plan.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, they oversold it like they oversell most things. I'd say it in the crib room rather than online, something like number 7 still needs me.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, though I know self-driving drills already exist at some mines. If it's all slow and boring, I think I've got a good fifteen years on this rig.
S0.do: Keeps working his usual drill shifts and keeps saving for a house deposit in his cheaper home town. Aims to grow about five months of savings to ten.
S0.feel: Calm, as if nothing has changed.
S0.quote: Didn't love that video, to be honest.
S0.fieldNote: He's attached to a specific machine and dislikes system changes, even a new tablet. His main plan is a house near his parents, which gives his saving a clear purpose. The video of a self-driving drill clearly stuck with him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. Yeah, that sounds more like it, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how things go, companies always find a cheaper way, and you can't stop it. But I'd also say the government should make sure people aren't just dumped. I'm not a big union guy, but I'd go to the meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my rig is one of the easier ones to automate. It's a plan with dots on it, and the machine follows the dots. I'd probably be fine for a few years, but I'd start to worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on anything new. No new car, keep saving. I'd probably wait to see if they actually start bringing in self-driving drills before I do anything else. If they do, I'd look at the smaller quarries nearby, where they won't spend that kind of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when the shift boss calls you in and you don't know why yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move from waiting to doing something?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw one of those rigs on site. Not a video, an actual one, parked by the workshop. That'd be my sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the smaller quarries. What would that mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less money, maybe twenty percent less, but a job. There's a limestone quarry about an hour from here, they still use old drills. I'd rather take less and keep doing what I know than go to a classroom.

S1.say: I'd say that's how it goes, because companies always find a cheaper way, but the government should make sure people aren't just dumped. I'd go to the union meeting even though I'm not a big union guy.
S1.think: I think my rig is one of the easier machines to automate, since it just follows dots on a plan. I'd probably be fine for a few years but I'd start to worry.
S1.do: Holds off on a new car and keeps saving. Waits to see whether self-driving drills actually arrive on site, and if they do, looks at smaller quarries nearby that are less likely to automate.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like being called into the shift boss's office without knowing why.
S1.quote: I'd rather take less and keep doing what I know than go to a classroom.
S1.fieldNote: He has a clear trigger for action, seeing a self-driving rig on site, and until then he'll wait. His escape route is sideways to a smaller, less automated quarry rather than retraining. His centre views show in accepting automation as business while wanting a basic safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one, AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? Righto. That's a hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and that someone should've seen it coming. I don't really blame the companies, they'd all be doing it, but the government should've had a plan. I'd say that to anyone at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm out of a job pretty quickly. If a robot can do anything, my drill is the first thing they'd swap. Even the quarries would get it eventually, it'd just cost less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard straight away, no more takeaway, no new phone, and cancel the trip to see my mates in the city. I'd keep working as long as they'd let me. If the job went, I'd probably move back in with Mum and Dad for a while and work on the farm next door to keep money coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I need my old room back for a bit. Dad would make a joke about it. Mum would be quietly worried, and that'd be worse than the joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the two years of warning help you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd save a few more months. But I'm not going to become something completely new in two years, I'm just not built like that.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and someone should have seen it coming. I don't really blame the companies, since they'd all do it, but the government should have had a plan.
S2.think: I think I'd be out of a job quickly, because my drill would be one of the first things swapped. Even the quarries would get it eventually.
S2.do: Cuts takeaways, a new phone and a planned trip straight away and keeps working as long as he's allowed. If the job goes, moves back in with his parents and works on a neighbouring farm for income.
S2.feel: Alarmed and lying awake at night.
S2.quote: Mum would be quietly worried, and that'd be worse than the joke.
S2.fieldNote: The fast timeline removes his usual fallback of a smaller quarry. He'd retreat to family and familiar farm work rather than try something new. He blames the lack of a government plan more than the companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now AGI by 2031. The same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit better, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's still fast, but at least there's some time. I'd want the company to tell us properly what's happening, not drop it on us in a meeting. And I'd say anyone young should start thinking now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have a few more years on the drill and then probably be out. I'd hate the idea of starting over, but five years would be long enough that I'd feel stupid not doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd keep saving and probably look for a job that's harder to automate, like at the quarry. If the mine offered training to look after the automated rigs, I'd probably take it, if it was close to what I do now. I'd hold off on the house deposit until I knew where I'd land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not like the two-year one, but it's sitting there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said close to what you do now. What would be too far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anything at a desk. I tried an office job for two months when I was nineteen, filing for a freight company. Hated every minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So would you take the training if it was at a desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, to be honest. Maybe if it paid really well. I'd rather look after the rigs out in the pit, even if I'm fixing one I used to drive.

S3.say: I'd say it's still fast, but at least there's some time. I'd want the company to tell us properly instead of dropping it on us in a meeting.
S3.think: I think I'd have a few more years on the drill and then probably be out. I'd hate starting over, but five years is long enough that doing nothing would feel stupid.
S3.do: Keeps saving and looks for a job that's harder to automate, such as at the quarry. Takes mine training to look after automated rigs if it's hands-on and close to his current work, and holds off on the house deposit.
S3.feel: Anxious, though less than with two years.
S3.quote: I tried an office job for two months when I was nineteen, filing for a freight company.
S3.fieldNote: Five years nudges him towards action, but only within narrow limits: hands-on, outdoors, close to drilling. He'd turn down a desk role unless the pay was very high. The house plan goes on hold, showing how uncertainty affects his biggest goal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fair warning, so nobody should be caught out. I'd also say a lot can change in ten years. They might not get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think ten years makes me lazy. I'd tell myself I'd sort it out later. I'd probably keep drilling for six or seven of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, keep saving, and probably go ahead with the house back home, because I'd have years to pay it down. I'd keep an eye on what's happening, and maybe around year five I'd look at a ticket for something else. Mostly I'd wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's far enough away to push to the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the ticket you'd look at, if you did?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a crane ticket, or something for the farm side. Machinery's what I know. I'd want something where I'm still in a seat with levers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said they might not get there. Do you actually believe that, or is it a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. I've heard about flying cars my whole life and I still drive a Hilux. But I know drills that run themselves already exist, so I'm not totally kidding myself.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is fair warning, so nobody should be caught out. I'd also say a lot can change and they might not get there.
S4.think: I think ten years would make me lazy, telling myself I'd sort it out later. I'd probably keep drilling for six or seven of those years.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving and goes ahead with buying a house back home. Waits and watches, considering a crane or farm machinery ticket around year five.
S4.feel: Uneasy but able to push it to the back of his mind.
S4.quote: I've heard about flying cars my whole life and I still drive a Hilux.
S4.fieldNote: The long timeline lets him go back to his default of waiting, and he admits it might make him lazy. He mixes real doubt about AGI with an awareness that automated drills already exist. Any new skill he'd consider still keeps him in a machine seat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is the mines being made to keep some people on for a while, and money to tide you over, so I'm not straight back in my old bedroom. And jobs out in the field, not desk courses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Probably about the dog. Sounds silly, but Rusty comes with me everywhere on my days off. If I lose the job and move home, at least he's got the farm. That's the one thing that'd be better.

headlineQuote: If I lose the job and move home, at least he's got the farm.
portrait: Liam is a 27-year-old blast hole drill operator at an iron ore mine who's driven the same rig, number 7, for four years and has about five months of savings. He's practical and in the middle politically, dislikes new systems and AI tools, and is saving for a house in his home town near his parents. He's calm in the plateau and waits and watches under steady change, ready to move to a less automated quarry. AGI in two years leaves him alarmed and heading back to his parents' place, while five and ten years let him think about hands-on work near what he knows, though he admits the long timeline might make him put things off.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he expects to lose his job quickly and end up back in his old bedroom.
whatWouldHelp: Requiring mines to keep some workers on for a while, money to tide people over, and hands-on field jobs instead of desk courses.
